summary:
North Maluku is a province of Indonesia and stands under the national framework: it has no separate criminalisation statute, no separate document regime and no recorded deviation from national policy material enough to score it apart. A trans visitor to North Maluku faces the legal position that applies across Indonesia.

Private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised nationally, but the penal code as amended on 6 December 2022 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage with effect from 2 January 2026. Unmarried partners face up to one year's imprisonment where an immediate family member lodges a complaint. Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, so all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. Reporting indicates that prosecutions under the provision are selective rather than systematic.

Legal gender recognition is available only after sex-reassignment surgery and judicial approval, and only male and female sex descriptors appear on Indonesian documents; there is no third-gender or X marker. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians electronic ID cards in nine provinces, which is the documentary route available to trans people resident in the country.

National law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and the Constitution is silent on sexual orientation and gender identity. On 14 December 2017 the Constitutional Court rejected a petition to criminalise homosexuality by five votes to four.

Criminalisation of same-sex conduct at provincial level is concentrated in Aceh, where Sharia law applies and where two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; South Sumatra also has provincial provisions targeting same-sex activity. These punishments reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. North Maluku is not among the provinces with their own criminalising provisions.

Enforcement elsewhere takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025 Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a violation of human rights and privacy.

There is a documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Peruvian trans student, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges in 2022 and died in custody; his mother alleges police beat him and that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release, while Indonesian police deny that violence was used.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. The Diplomat reported in August 2026 that Indonesia's transgender community faces growing repression, with vigilante mobs attacking trans people while the government takes steps to codify anti-LGBT provisions into law. Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, and a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
North Maluku's position is defined by national law rather than provincial initiative, so the turbulence to watch is national: the October 2025 presidential decree placing LGBTQ+ people inside defence policy, and the wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women reported in August 2026, both apply to the province without any local instrument of their own.

The comparison that matters for a visitor is between provinces. Aceh operates a separate Sharia-based regime with public caning, and South Sumatra has its own provisions; the rest of the country, North Maluku included, relies on the national penal code's outside-marriage offence. A visitor moving between provinces therefore crosses between enforcement regimes.

Public opinion is markedly hostile: a 2023 Pew Research survey found 95% of Indonesians oppose same-sex marriage, and Indonesia's vote against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity indicates the direction of official diplomacy. Neither is a legal prohibition, but both bear on the risk of reporting a crime or seeking assistance.

Arrest risk for trans visitors has historically attached to drug charges and to venue raids rather than to gender presentation alone, as the 2022 custody death and the June 2025 villa raid illustrate.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for Indonesian residents requires sex-reassignment surgery followed by judicial approval, and the resulting documents carry only male or female sex descriptors.

Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run an outreach programme issuing electronic ID cards to transgender Indonesians in nine provinces. Whether North Maluku is among those nine provinces is not stated in the sources available here.

Residents have no statutory anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the Constitution does not mention either. The Constitutional Court's 5-4 refusal on 14 December 2017 to criminalise homosexuality closed the most direct route to expanded criminal liability, leaving the outside-marriage provision of the amended penal code as the operative instrument.

Provincial religious law in Aceh applies to anyone within that province, including Indonesian residents returning from elsewhere; it does not extend to North Maluku.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records a specific enforcement action, arrest, raid or prosecution of a trans person within North Maluku itself. The province-level picture here is derived from national law and national reporting, and any North Maluku-specific incident would be unresolved on the present record.

Whether North Maluku has its own regional regulations (peraturan daerah) on morality, dress or public order that could be used against trans people is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Whether North Maluku is one of the nine provinces covered by the Ministry of Home Affairs electronic ID outreach is not stated in the sources and is unresolved.

The sources do not establish how often the outside-marriage provision has been used against same-sex couples since it took effect on 2 January 2026, nor whether the selective pattern of prosecution reported nationally holds in this province.
